note: New authoring source for the next integration batch. Journeys carry arcs only; cadence is intentionally absent.

families.goal: Build a job search I can keep going

axis.placementQuestion: Which kind of search is most realistic for you to keep going: a very explicit process, a simple weekly rhythm, or a flexible minimum that still works in a busy week?

journeys.title: Build a job-search pipeline you can repeat
journeys.description: Turn the search into a small explicit process, find the point that breaks, simplify it, and create a minimum version for busy weeks.

milestones.title: I have a simple, explicit search process
I ran it once and found where it breaks
I simplified one weak point and ran it again
I have a minimum version for a busy week

steps.title: Write the four stages of your search
steps.description: Finding opportunities, checking fit, applying or reaching out, and following up is enough.

steps.title: Choose one small weekly target for each stage
steps.description: Set targets for a normal week, not an ideal one.

steps.title: Run the process once
steps.description: The goal is to test the process, not to do a large volume of searching.

steps.title: Mark where the process broke down
steps.description: Choose one bottleneck, not five.

steps.title: Simplify one stage
steps.description: Use a template, a short checklist, or a clearer rule for what you will not pursue.

steps.title: Run the process again
steps.description: Check whether the revised version is easier to execute.

steps.title: Define the minimum version for a busy week
steps.description: What is the smallest version that keeps the search alive without creating overload?

journeys.title: Build a simple weekly job-search rhythm
journeys.description: Replace a complicated system with two small search moments you can realistically repeat.

milestones.title: I chose two realistic search moments
I completed one full week of that rhythm
I adjusted one thing based on what worked
I have a rhythm I can keep using

steps.title: Choose two realistic search moments
steps.description: Pick windows that are likely to happen in your real week.

steps.title: Give each moment one job
steps.description: For example: one moment to find and filter, one to apply or reach out.

steps.title: Do both search moments this week
steps.description: Missing one does not turn the week into a reset.

steps.title: Notice what made one moment easier than the other
steps.description: Time of day, task type, preparation, or something else.

steps.title: Change one detail only
steps.description: Do not redesign the whole rhythm.

steps.title: Do the two search moments again
steps.description: Check whether the adjusted rhythm is easier to keep.

steps.title: Choose the rhythm you will carry forward
steps.description: Decide what stays stable and what is allowed to move.

journeys.title: Keep the search alive even in a very busy week
journeys.description: Start from a minimum action that is genuinely sustainable, then add only when capacity is available.

milestones.title: I defined one minimum search action
I kept the search alive without overloading the week
I adjusted the minimum to what is actually sustainable
I have a return rule after a missed week

steps.title: Choose a search action that takes ten minutes or less
steps.description: Pick something small enough to keep the search alive.

steps.title: Do it once
steps.description: The minimum counts as success on its own.

steps.title: Add one more action only if there is capacity
steps.description: Do not turn a good week into the new minimum.

steps.title: Write down what was actually possible
steps.description: Use the time and energy you really had, not what you hoped to have.

steps.title: Adjust the minimum if it is still too large
steps.description: The minimum is supposed to protect continuity, not prove commitment.

steps.title: Use the same rule in another week
steps.description: Minimum first; add more only if the week allows it.

steps.title: Write a return rule for a missed week
steps.description: Return to the minimum instead of trying to make up everything you missed.

families.goal: Get better at interviews when I am reaching interviews but not progressing

axis.placementQuestion: What would help you learn most right now: analyzing a real interview, practicing your answers, or preparing a small bank of strong examples from your experience?

journeys.title: Learn from a real interview and improve one pattern
journeys.description: Reconstruct a recent interview, separate evidence from guesses, choose one pattern to change, and test that change in the next interview.

milestones.title: I reconstructed one recent interview
I identified one interview pattern worth changing
I practiced one targeted change
I tested the change in a real interview

steps.title: Reconstruct the last interview in three moments
steps.description: One moment that went well, one that felt weak, and one question that surprised you.

steps.title: Separate what you know from what you are guessing
steps.description: For example, 'I spoke for four minutes' is evidence; 'they were bored' is a guess.

steps.title: Compare with any real feedback you have
steps.description: If you have no feedback, do not invent it.

steps.title: Choose one pattern to improve
steps.description: For example: answers that run too long, weak examples, or unclear structure.

steps.title: Prepare one small change
steps.description: For example: a three-part answer structure or one stronger example.

steps.title: Practice one or two questions with the change
steps.description: A short rehearsal is enough.

steps.title: Use the change in your next interview
steps.description: Measure whether the pattern changed, not only whether you got an offer.

journeys.title: Improve interview performance through short practice
journeys.description: Create a baseline, improve one answer at a time, get focused feedback, and use the new structure in a real interview.

milestones.title: I created a baseline for two interview answers
I improved the clarity and evidence in one answer
I practiced and got focused feedback
I used the change in a real interview

steps.title: Choose two interview questions that keep coming up
steps.description: Use questions you have actually been asked.

steps.title: Answer both once without special preparation
steps.description: This is your baseline.

steps.title: Check one answer for three things
steps.description: Is it clear, focused, and supported by a concrete example?

steps.title: Build a shorter version of that answer
steps.description: Keep the story true; remove details that do not help the point.

steps.title: Practice the two questions again
steps.description: See whether you can get to the point faster.

steps.title: Ask one person for focused feedback on one answer
steps.description: Ask what they understood about your ability from the answer.

steps.title: Use the structure in your next interview
steps.description: Right after the interview, note whether it was easier to stay focused.

journeys.title: Build a small bank of examples you can retrieve under pressure
journeys.description: Organize real experience around the abilities the target role looks for, then practice retrieving the right example when the question changes.

milestones.title: I mapped real examples to the abilities the target role requires
I turned those examples into concise interview evidence
I practiced retrieving the right example for different questions
I used at least one example in a real interview

steps.title: Choose three abilities that repeat across your target roles
steps.description: For example: stakeholder management, prioritization, or process improvement.

steps.title: Find one real story for each ability
steps.description: Use an example with your action and a real outcome or change.

steps.title: Reduce each story to four parts
steps.description: Context, your action, a trade-off or decision, and the result or learning.

steps.title: Choose the weakest story
steps.description: Do not rewrite all of them at once.

steps.title: Strengthen it with evidence you already have
steps.description: Add a concrete decision, action, or outcome without inventing numbers.

steps.title: Practice retrieving the stories from different questions
steps.description: The goal is flexible retrieval, not memorization.

steps.title: Use at least one story in your next interview
steps.description: Afterward, note whether it was easier to retrieve a strong example in the moment.

families.goal: Return to action after repeated rejection

axis.placementQuestion: What would help you return to action most: starting extremely small, following a short explicit return path, or rebuilding one piece of competence evidence before going back out?

journeys.title: Return to the search through actions small enough to start
journeys.description: Restore movement before trying to fix the whole search, then create a simple return rule for the next rejection.

milestones.title: I returned to one small search action
I proved I can restart without a burst of effort
I carried a small search rhythm into another period
I have a return rule for the next rejection

steps.title: Choose one search action that takes ten minutes or less
steps.description: Pick something small enough that it does not require getting fully 'back into search mode'.

steps.title: Do it once
steps.description: The goal is movement, not fixing the entire search.

steps.title: Choose one more action at the same difficulty
steps.description: Keep it deliberately small.

steps.title: Do that action too
steps.description: Notice what was easier than you expected.

steps.title: Choose two short search moments for the next period
steps.description: Do not raise the load quickly just because restarting went well.

steps.title: Complete at least one of them
steps.description: Missing the other one is not a reset.

steps.title: Write your return rule for the next rejection
steps.description: Return to one small action instead of trying to compensate for everything.

journeys.title: Return to the search through a short, explicit restart path
journeys.description: Choose two familiar return actions, complete them without compensating for lost time, and carry one small action into the next period.

milestones.title: I have a two-action return path
I completed both return actions without trying to make up everything I missed
I carried the search into another period at a small load
I have a clear return rule for the next rejection

steps.title: Choose two search actions you already know how to do
steps.description: For example: one outreach and checking two roles. Do not add a new preparation project.

steps.title: Put them in the order that is easiest to start
steps.description: The goal is a simple entry path, not a full search plan.

steps.title: Complete the first return action
steps.description: Do not add extra actions to make up for lost time.

steps.title: Complete the second return action
steps.description: Keep it the same size even if the week is busy.

steps.title: Choose one search action for the next period
steps.description: Keep it small enough that it does not require a burst of motivation.

steps.title: Complete the action you chose
steps.description: The goal is continuity into another period, not higher volume.

steps.title: Write the return rule you will use next time
steps.description: For example: after a rejection, return to one of the two known actions instead of trying to compensate for everything.

journeys.title: Rebuild one piece of competence evidence, then return to the market
journeys.description: Restore a concrete sense of capability through one small proof action, then reconnect it immediately to real search activity.

milestones.title: I identified evidence that my capability did not disappear with the rejection
I created one small, usable piece of competence evidence
I used it in a real search action
I returned to outward action with a rule that protects competence

steps.title: Choose one thing from the recent search that still proves growth or capability
steps.description: For example: an interview you reached, a skill you used, a connection you built, or a piece of work you improved.

steps.title: Choose one small competence action you control
steps.description: Pick something that can produce evidence, not just more preparation.

steps.title: Bring it to a usable version
steps.description: Aim for usable, not perfect.

steps.title: Use it in one real search action
steps.description: Do not let preparation become avoidance.

steps.title: Notice what changed in your sense of readiness
steps.description: You do not need fear or doubt to disappear before acting.

steps.title: Do one more outward search action
steps.description: Keep the load small enough to remain sustainable.

steps.title: Choose one rule for protecting competence during rejection
steps.description: For example: use one small proof-building action when needed, without stopping the search itself.
